title: Consistency Models
tagline: Strong, eventual, causal, read-your-writes — what each promises and when 'good enough' is good enough.
summary: Strong vs eventual consistency and the useful models in between.

paragraphs: The moment you replicate data across multiple nodes (for scale and availability), a hard question appears: if you write to one copy, what do *other* copies return before the update propagates? **Consistency models** are the precise contracts that answer 'which value will a reader see, and when?'.

It's a spectrum. At one end, **strong consistency** behaves as if there's a single up-to-date copy — every read sees the latest write. At the other, **eventual consistency** only promises that *if writes stop, all replicas converge to the same value eventually*. In between sit several practical models. Stronger guarantees cost latency and availability; weaker ones buy speed and uptime.

blocks.text: Think of a shared Google Doc vs a group chat rumor. The Doc shows everyone the same latest text the instant it's typed (strong). A rumor spreads person to person — for a while different people 'know' different versions, but eventually everyone hears the final story (eventual).

items.detail: Every read returns the most recent committed write; the system behaves like one copy. Easiest to reason about, but requires coordination (slower, and unavailable during partitions). Needed for bank balances, inventory, unique usernames.
Replicas may temporarily disagree but converge if writes stop. Fast and highly available. Fine for like counts, view counts, social feeds, DNS.

A user always sees their *own* updates immediately, even if others see them later. Prevents the jarring 'I posted but it vanished' bug. Often done by routing a user's reads to the primary or their own session's replica.
Once you've seen a value, you won't later see an *older* one (no going back in time). Prevents data 'flickering' between versions across requests.

Operations that are causally related (a reply must come after its message) are seen in the right order everywhere, while unrelated operations may be seen in any order. A practical middle ground for chat/comments.

blocks.text: Most large systems are *not* uniformly strong or eventual — they pick consistency per data type. Strong for money and inventory; eventual for counters and feeds; read-your-writes for a user's own profile edits. Saying this in an interview signals maturity.

rows: Can't sell the same seat twice
Two people can't claim the same handle
Off-by-a-few for a moment is harmless
Your own post must appear; others can lag

blocks.title: The trade-off to verbalise
blocks.text: 'Strong consistency requires cross-node coordination, which adds latency and forces a choice between consistency and availability during a network partition (CAP). Where users can tolerate brief staleness, I'll choose eventual consistency to keep the system fast and always-on, and reserve strong consistency for data where correctness is non-negotiable.'

cheatsheet: Consistency models define which value a reader sees after a write across replicas.
Strong = always latest (needs coordination, slower, less available); eventual = converges if writes stop (fast, available).
Useful middles: read-your-writes, monotonic reads, causal consistency.
Pick consistency *per data type*: strong for money/inventory/unique IDs; eventual for counts/feeds.
Stronger consistency trades latency + availability; this is the heart of the CAP theorem.

questions.prompt: A user updates their profile bio, refreshes, and sees the OLD bio. Which consistency guarantee is missing, and how do you fix it without making the whole system strongly consistent?
questions.hint: They need to see their own writes — but others can lag.
answer: The missing guarantee is **read-your-own-writes**. Their write went to the primary, but their refresh read from a replica that hadn't received the update yet (replication lag).

Fix it narrowly instead of making everything strong: route a user's reads to the primary for a short window after they write, or pin their reads to a replica known to be caught up, or read from a write-through cache updated on their write. This gives that user immediate consistency for their own data while everyone else can still read cheaply from lagging replicas (eventual).
keyPoints: Route own reads to primary / caught-up replica / write-through cache
Keep others eventual — don't make everything strong

questions.prompt: Give one example each where eventual consistency is perfectly fine and where it is dangerous.
questions.hint: Where does a brief disagreement between replicas matter to correctness?
answer: Fine: a YouTube view count or a tweet's like count. If two replicas briefly show 1,000 vs 1,003, no one is harmed and they'll converge. The win is speed and always-on availability.

Dangerous: a bank account balance or remaining flight seats. If two replicas disagree, you could allow a double withdrawal or sell the same seat twice. These need strong consistency (or at least a single authoritative decision point) so a write is globally agreed before it's acted on.
keyPoints: Fine for counts/feeds where brief disagreement is harmless
Dangerous for money/inventory where it causes double-spend/oversell
The distinguisher is whether stale reads cause incorrect actions
followUps: How would you make just the 'decrement seats' operation strongly consistent in an otherwise eventual system?
